H1.text: A bus goes all around the city and back to its depot. A runner finishes four laps of the track.

H2.text: Both travel a long way. And both end up exactly where they started.

H3.text: Aarav rides his bicycle to the shop, one kilometre away, and comes straight back home.

H4.text: His trip meter says two kilometres. But his physics teacher says he moved zero. Who is right?

H5.text: Both of them. They measure two different things. Let's see which.

P1.text: The first one is distance. Distance is the length of the actual path you travel.

P2.text: Every bend and every turn counts. It only has a size, so distance is a scalar.

P3.text: The second one is displacement. It is the straight arrow from where you start to where you end.

P4.text: It has a size and a direction, so displacement is a vector. It does not care which path you took.

S1.text: Let's watch one ride on a straight road. Home is at zero.

S2.text: This time Aarav rides forward to the library, six hundred metres away.

S3.text: Up to here, distance and displacement are both six hundred metres. They grow together.

S4.text: Now he turns back and rides four hundred metres to his friend's house.

S5.text: Watch the graph. Distance keeps climbing. Displacement starts to fall.

S6.text: Let's replay the turn in slow motion.

S7.text: The wheels keep rolling, so the path adds up. But the arrow from home gets shorter.

S8.text: Final count. Distance is one thousand metres. Displacement is two hundred metres, forward.

D1.text: Let's write this as a rule, one step at a time.

D2.text: Step one. Distance s is the sum of every piece of the path. Six hundred plus four hundred. One thousand metres.

D3.text: Step two. Displacement is final position minus starting position. Two hundred minus zero, two hundred metres.

D4.text: Step three. So the size of the displacement is never more than the distance.

T1.text: Remember this. Distance is the whole path. Displacement is the straight shortcut.

C1.text: But why can distance never be smaller? Let's follow the reasoning, link by link.

C2.text: Link one. Between two points, a straight line is the shortest path.

C3.text: Link two. Displacement is exactly that straight line, from start to end.

C4.text: Link three. Any real path is that line, or something longer with bends and turns.

C5.text: So distance is always at least the size of displacement. Equal only on a straight path with no turning back.

K1.text: Side by side. Distance is a scalar. It is never negative, and it never goes down.

K2.text: Displacement is a vector. It can be positive, negative, or zero. Only the start and the end matter.

K3.text: Now you try. Aarav cycles once around a round park and stops where he began. Is his displacement zero? Pause and decide.

K4.text: Yes, zero! He ends where he started. But his distance is the whole way around the park.

V1.text: Let's test this on a circle.

V2.text: A dot moves around a circle of radius r. Violet arc: distance. Blue arrow: displacement.

V3.text: After a quarter turn, the distance is pi r by two. The displacement is root two times r.

V4.text: After half a turn, distance is pi r. Displacement is two r, straight across, its biggest value.

V5.text: After a full turn, the distance is two pi r. The displacement drops back to zero.

V6.text: Your turn. On any path, can the distance ever be less than the size of the displacement? Pause and decide.

V7.text: Never! The displacement is the straight line, and nothing is shorter than a straight line.

W2.text: Aarav cycles half way around a round park of radius seventy metres. Find the distance and the displacement.

W3.text: Distance is half the circumference. So s equals pi r.

W4.text: With pi as twenty two by seven, s is twenty two by seven times seventy. Two hundred and twenty metres.

W5.text: Displacement is the straight line across the park, the diameter. So it equals two r.

W6.text: Two times seventy. One hundred and forty metres.

X2.text: Many students say that after one full round, the displacement is two pi r.

X3.text: But two pi r is the distance. After one full round you are back at the start, so the displacement is zero.

E1.text: Where is this asked? Short questions on round trips and circles: distance, displacement, or their ratio.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A particle goes three quarters of the way around a circle of radius R. Find distance over the size of displacement. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is A. Three pi, over two root two.

A2.text: Distance is three quarters of two pi R. That is three pi R by two.

A3.text: Start and end are ninety degrees apart, so the displacement is root two R.

A4.text: Divide. Three pi R by two, over root two R, gives three pi over two root two. About three point three.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Can the distance be zero while the displacement is not?

Y3.text: Two. When are distance and displacement exactly equal?

Y4.text: Three. What is the displacement after half a lap of a circle of radius r?

N1.text: Next time: two cyclists, same speed, opposite directions. Same speed, but different velocity? That is speed and velocity.
